title: The imperfect: habits and descriptions
objectives: I can explain, from the stress rule and the spelling rules, why the imperfect forms are written as they are, for example why falávamos and íamos carry an accent while falava and ia do not.
I can explain the difference between the imperfect, which sees the past from inside as ongoing or repeated, and the preterite, which sees an event as a completed whole.
I can form the pretérito imperfeito of regular verbs and of the four irregular verbs ser, ter, vir and pôr.
I can talk about my childhood and past habits with quando eu era criança, antigamente and naquela época, and use costumava plus an infinitive.
I can describe past scenes, ages, time and weather using the imperfect.
I can say what was going on at a given moment with estava plus a gerund, and form the gerund of any regular verb.

vocabulary.note: Infância is stressed on the third to last syllable (in-FÂN-ci-a, with the ending ia counted as two syllables), and a stress there always needs a written accent. The circumflex â also shows that the stressed a, which comes before n, is closed and nasal. The ci is said like s.

example.pt: Tive uma infância muito feliz.
example.en: I had a very happy childhood.

vocabulary.note: Colégio is also common, especially for private schools. The sc before o is two sounds in a row, s and then k: es-CO-la.

example.pt: Eu ia a pé pra escola todo dia.
example.en: I walked to school every day.
example.literal: I went at foot to-the school all day.

vocabulary.note: Portuguese says literally a lesson of house where English says homework; fazer (to make or do) is the verb that goes with it. Dever de casa and tarefa mean the same. In lição, the ç is the s sound before ã, and the ending ão is stressed by default: li-ÇÃO.

example.pt: Eu fazia a lição de casa depois do almoço.
example.en: I did my homework after lunch.
example.literal: I made the lesson of house after of-the lunch.

vocabulary.note: From brincar. Pega-pega is the game of tag: pega is the verb pegar (to catch) in the he or she form, said twice and joined by a hyphen into one name. A brincadeira can also be a joke, and Brincadeira! on its own means just kidding.

example.pt: Pega-pega era a nossa brincadeira preferida.
example.en: Tag was our favorite game.
example.literal: Catch-catch was the our game preferred.

vocabulary.note: Brincar is for children's play and for joking. For sports and games use jogar, and for instruments use tocar. The c of brincar is the k sound; in the imperfect brincava it stays c because a follows, while before e it becomes qu (brinquei, from the preterite unit).

example.pt: A gente brincava na rua até escurecer.
example.en: We played in the street until it got dark.
example.literal: The-people played in-the street until to-get-dark.

vocabulary.note: The qu before i is the k sound and its u is silent. The final l is said like w, so quintal sounds like kin-TAW, and since l is an ending that defaults to a stressed last syllable, no accent is needed. Mangueira, the mango tree, is explained in the note on spelling and sound.

example.pt: A casa tinha um quintal enorme com uma mangueira.
example.en: The house had a huge backyard with a mango tree.

vocabulary.note: Desenho animado is the standard word and is often shortened to desenho. The nh in desenho is the sound of ny in canyon, and the adjective animado follows its noun. In careful speech assistir takes the preposition a (assistir a), and everyday speech often drops it.

example.pt: Eu assistia a desenhos animados todo sábado de manhã.
example.en: I watched cartoons every Saturday morning.
example.literal: I attended-to drawings animated all Saturday of morning.

vocabulary.note: In Brazil o interior means everything outside the capital and the large metropolitan area of a state, so it includes towns of any size and not only farmland. It ends in r, which defaults to a stressed last syllable, so there is no accent: in-te-ri-OR.

example.pt: Meus avós moravam no interior de Minas.
example.en: My grandparents lived in the interior of Minas.

vocabulary.note: O sítio is a small rural property with a house and some land, smaller than a fazenda, and often used for weekends and holidays. Sítio is stressed on the third to last syllable (SÍ-ti-o, io counted as two), so it has an acute accent, and the t is said tch because it comes before i.

example.pt: A gente passava as férias no sítio da minha avó.
example.en: We spent our vacations at my grandmother's country house.
example.literal: The-people passed the vacations in-the farm of-the my grandmother.

vocabulary.note: Rr between vowels is the strong h-like sound, and ai is one syllable (a diphthong): BAI-hru. Todo mundo, literally all world, is the everyday way to say everybody.

example.pt: No meu bairro todo mundo se conhecia.
example.en: In my neighborhood everyone knew each other.
example.literal: In-the my neighborhood all world themselves knew.

vocabulary.note: Saudade is the feeling of missing a person, a place or a time, with a mix of sweetness and sadness. It is used as ter saudade de, to miss, and as the exclamation Que saudade! It is usually traced to Latin solitas, solitude, and English has no single word for it. The au is a diphthong, so the word has three syllables, sau-DA-de; compare saúde, where the accent keeps the u separate.

example.pt: Tenho muita saudade da minha infância.
example.en: I miss my childhood a lot.
example.literal: I-have much longing of-the my childhood.

vocabulary.note: Lembrar takes de (da is de plus a), or the reflexive form: Eu lembro dela and Eu me lembro dela both mean I remember her. The em before b is a nasal vowel, and the br has a tap r: lem-BRAR.

example.pt: Eu lembro da cor da minha primeira bicicleta.
example.en: I remember the color of my first bicycle.
example.literal: I remember of-the color of-the my first bicycle.

vocabulary.note: Antigamente is built from antiga, the feminine of antigo, plus the ending -mente, which turns an adjective into an adverb like English -ly. It is stressed on men: an-ti-ga-MEN-te.

example.pt: Antigamente, as pessoas escreviam cartas.
example.en: In the old days, people wrote letters.

vocabulary.note: Naquela is em (in) fused with aquela (that, for something distant in time), the same kind of contraction as na (em plus a); with de the result is daquele and daquela. Época is stressed on the third to last syllable (É-po-ca), so it has an acute accent, which also shows the open e.

example.pt: Naquela época, não tinha internet.
example.en: Back then, there was no internet.

vocabulary.note: Antigo means old in the sense of from long ago. For an elderly person use velho or idoso. It agrees with its noun: antigo, antiga, antigos, antigas. The g is hard because it comes before o or a.

example.pt: Tenho umas fotos muito antigas da minha cidade.
example.en: I have some very old photos of my town.

vocabulary.note: Crescer means to grow, and in the past it often means to grow up. The sc before e is a single s sound (a leftover of the Latin spelling), as in nascer, to be born: cres-CER, eu cresci, eu nasci.

example.pt: Eu cresci numa cidade pequena do interior.
example.en: I grew up in a small town in the interior.
example.literal: I grew in-a city small of-the interior.

vocabulary.note: From costume, a custom or habit. English costume (an outfit) is fantasia or traje in Portuguese, so the two are partly false friends. Costumar is followed directly by an infinitive, with no preposition. In the present it means usually (eu costumo acordar cedo) and in the imperfect it means used to (eu costumava acordar cedo).

example.pt: Eu costumava acordar às seis da manhã.
example.en: I used to wake up at six in the morning.
example.literal: I was-accustomed to-wake at-the six of-the morning.

vocabulary.note: A fixed phrase whose four words never change. Vez is an occasion or a time, as in uma vez (once). The qu in quando is followed by a, so the u is pronounced like w.

example.pt: De vez em quando a gente ia ao cinema.
example.en: From time to time we went to the cinema.
example.literal: Of time in when the-people went to-the cinema.

vocabulary.note: Fixo is the adjective fixed, in contrast with o celular (the mobile phone). The x in fixo is the sound ks: FI-ksu.

example.pt: Antigamente a gente só tinha telefone fixo.
example.en: In the old days we only had a landline.
example.literal: Oldly the-people only had telephone fixed.

vocabulary.note: Carta is a letter sent by mail. A letter of the alphabet is uma letra, so the English word letter covers two Portuguese words.

example.pt: Minha avó escrevia uma carta toda semana.
example.en: My grandmother wrote a letter every week.

vocabulary.note: Short for Nossa Senhora, Our Lady, but now a general exclamation of surprise, admiration or dismay with no religious tone. The ss between vowels is the s sound: NO-sa.

example.pt: Nossa, que diferente!
example.en: Wow, how different!

vocabulary.note: Said to agree, often with a hint of yes, I know, that is how it is. Pois is a filler meaning well or so, and é (is) carries an accent because it is a one-syllable word that ends in e and is stressed; without the accent, e would mean and.

example.pt: Pois é, antigamente era diferente.
example.en: That's right, in the old days it was different.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the new words and verb forms of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Nothing in this unit's spelling is new. Every accent and every unusual letter below follows a rule from the first three lessons, and this note shows those rules at work on the new words so that you can read and write them instead of memorizing them. Two questions solve almost every word. First, where is the stress, and does it agree with the default for the word's ending? Words ending in a, e or o (with or without s) and in am, em or ens are stressed on the second to last syllable, and most other endings are stressed on the last syllable. When the stress disagrees with the default, a written accent appears on the stressed vowel. Second, what do the neighboring letters say about how a letter is pronounced? The letter c, the pairs qu and gu, and a vowel followed by m or n are all decided by what surrounds them, while nh, lh, ch and rr are digraphs, two letters that together stand for one sound.

The largest group of accents in this unit sits on the verb forms of the imperfect, the past tense this unit teaches (the next notes define it), and one rule explains all of them. A verb form in this unit keeps its stress on the same vowel however it is extended. In falava the stress is on the a after the l (fa-LA-va), and in falavam it is still there. The nós form adds one more syllable, so the stress ends up third from the end: fa-LÁ-va-mos. A word ending in os is expected to be stressed on the second to last syllable, so a stress on the third to last breaks the default and takes an accent (and a stress that far back always needs one, because no ending predicts it). Compare the present falamos, fa-LA-mos, whose stress is second to last and which needs no accent. The same reasoning produces comíamos, abríamos, íamos, éramos, tínhamos, vínhamos, púnhamos and estávamos. The accent on é in éramos is the acute of an open vowel, while on í and ú it only marks stress, because i and u have just one sound.

The singular forms show the other side. Comia (co-MI-a) ends in a and is stressed on the second to last syllable, which is the default, so it has no accent, and ia (I-a) is the same. A second reason for accents appears in saía, the form of sair meaning he or she used to leave. Its stressed i follows the vowel a, and a stressed i or u that follows another vowel in this way stands alone in its syllable and is written í or ú: sa-Í-a. The accent shows that the i is not the quick glide of a diphthong, exactly as in país and saúde. Without it, saia would be read as sai-a, which is the word for a skirt.

The other new words apply the consonant rules. The pair gu before e keeps the g hard, which is why the mango tree is mangueira and not mangeira: manga is the fruit, the ending -eira makes a tree, and ge would be read zhe, so a silent u is inserted. It is the same logic as brincar becoming brinquei in the preterite. The pairs nh and lh are single sounds (tinha, vizinho, filha, olha), rr is the strong h-like sound (bairro, cachorro), the sc before e or i is a plain s (crescer, nasci), and the final l is said like w (quintal). The plural verb ending -am is the nasal glide from the nasal vowel lesson, said weakly when unstressed: falavam, eram. Loan words keep their original spelling and do not follow the stress defaults, so internet is said in-ter-NÉ-tchi, with a final i sound added.

Use the table as a checklist. Each row names a pattern, the words in this unit that show it and the reason for the spelling. When you meet a new word with an accent, do not ask whether to learn the accent; count syllables, find the stress and compare it with the default.

headers: Why it is written this way
rows: falávamos, comíamos, íamos, éramos, tínhamos, estávamos
Stress on the third to last syllable always takes an accent. The singular falava, comia, ia, era has second to last stress, which is the default.
A stressed i after another vowel stands alone in its syllable and takes an accent, so it is not read as a diphthong. Compare saia, the skirt.
infância, época, sítio, férias, árvores, rápido, prédio, aniversário

All are stressed on the third to last syllable, with ia, io and ias counted as two syllables, so each needs an accent. An acute accent marks an open vowel (or just the stress, on i and u) and a circumflex marks a closed one.
Circumflex ô is the closed o, as in ônibus and avô. Vovô ends in o with the stress on the last syllable, which breaks the default.
A stressed one-syllable word that ends in a, e or o takes an accent. Né is não é squeezed into one syllable, and a pé means on foot.
Each is stressed on the last syllable although its ending (as, em, e) defaults to second to last, so it takes an accent. The oi in Goiás is a diphthong.
Ç is the s sound before a, o and u. In lição the ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, and the tilde makes it nasal. An before a consonant is a nasal vowel.
Qu before e or i is usually the k sound with a silent u (a few words such as tranquilo and cinquenta pronounce it); before a or o the u is pronounced like w (quando). The final l is said like w.
Gu before e is a hard g with a silent u. Manga is the fruit and -eira makes the tree.
Nh is one sound, like ny in canyon.
Lh is one sound, like lli in million.
Rr is the strong h-like sound, and ch is sh.
Sc before e or i is a single s sound. Before a, o or u it is two sounds, s and k: escola, escurecer.
Au is a diphthong in one syllable, so saudade has three syllables. Saúde, with an accent, keeps a and u apart.
The ending am is the nasal glide said weakly. It defaults to second to last stress, so no accent is needed. Compare têm, they have.
An, en and in before a consonant are nasal vowels, and the n is not pronounced as a consonant. The stress is second to last, so no accent.
G before e is zh, h is silent and j is zh, and c before e is s. A final unstressed e is said i, and t before that i is tch.
A loan word from English, with its spelling kept and a final i sound added when it is read in Portuguese.

grammar.title: What the imperfect means and how regular verbs form it
grammar.explanation:
Two ideas have to be separated before the forms make sense. A tense says when something happened, and an aspect says how the speaker looks at the action. The same past event can be seen from outside, as one whole completed event with a beginning and an end, or from inside, as something that was going on, used to go on or formed the background of a scene. Portuguese has two simple past tenses that differ by aspect and not by time. The preterite (pretérito perfeito, the previous units) is the outside view: falei, I spoke, and that was that. The imperfect (pretérito imperfeito) is the inside view: falava. The word imperfect is Latin for not completed, and it means that the speaker does not say how or when the action ended.

English has no single tense for the inside view, so it uses different devices depending on the meaning: the simple past (I lived there), used to (I used to play), would (I would play every day) and was plus -ing (I was playing). Portuguese uses one form for all of them, and the context chooses the translation. That is why Eu jogava bola todo dia can be translated as I played ball every day, I used to play ball every day or I would play ball every day.

The regular forms are simple. Remove the infinitive ending (-ar, -er or -ir) to get the stem, then add -ava for -ar verbs (fal-ava) and -ia for -er and -ir verbs (com-ia, abr-ia). These endings are the old Latin endings with the b worn down to v or lost altogether. A useful way to remember them is that the -v- marks the -ar family and the -i- marks the other two, so in the imperfect the -er and -ir verbs, which differ in the preterite and the present, share one set of endings. Ir, to go, takes the -ia ending directly (eu ia, ele ia, eles iam), and ver and ler are regular (via, lia).

Two practical consequences follow. First, the eu form and the form for você, ele, ela and a gente are identical (eu falava, ele falava), unlike the preterite where falei and falou differ, so the subject pronoun is used more often in the imperfect to avoid confusion. Second, the stress never falls on the last syllable of an imperfect form, unlike falei or falou: it sits on the a of -ava or on the i of -ia, which is why falava and comia need no accent. The nós form adds a syllable and receives an accent for the reasons in the spelling note: falávamos, comíamos, abríamos, íamos. In everyday speech a gente falava (the same form as ele) is much more common than nós falávamos.

grammar.title: The four irregular verbs: ser, ter, vir and pôr
grammar.explanation:
Only four verbs are irregular in the imperfect: ser (to be), ter (to have), vir (to come) and pôr (to put). They are not irregular in their endings so much as in the shape of the stem, and the pattern is the same for all four. In the regular imperfect the ending carries a visible -v- or -i-. In these four verbs that syllable has disappeared, so the endings are just -a, -a, -amos and -am attached to a changed stem: er- for ser, tinh- for ter, vinh- for vir and pun- for pôr. Pôr descends from the older infinitive poer, so it historically belongs with the -er verbs, but its imperfect stem pun- simply has to be learned.

These four verbs are among the most frequent in the language, and compounds follow the verb they are built on: manter becomes mantinha, conter becomes continha, convir becomes convinha, compor becomes compunha. Ter and vir keep the nh sound seen in the spelling note, and their nós forms are tínhamos and vínhamos with an acute accent on the i, for the stress reason explained there. Do not confuse vinha (from vir, came) with via (from ver, saw): the first has the nh stem, the second is regular.

Ser is the most important of the four because it is the verb of description: A casa era grande, Eu era tímido. Ter is the verb of age and of possession, and it also does the work of there was, as the next note shows.

grammar.title: The jobs of the imperfect: habit, description, background, age, time and weather
grammar.explanation:
Because the imperfect views the past from inside, with no beginning or end in sight, it fits every situation in which the end is irrelevant or does not exist. The traditional list has five or six uses, but they are one idea. Repeated actions and habits have no single end (Eu brincava na rua todo dia). Descriptions of people, places and things are states, and a state has no moment of ending in the story (A casa era grande). Background situations are what was going on while something else happens (Meu pai trabalhava num banco). Age, the time of day and the weather are states of the world at that moment: Eu tinha dez anos, Eram duas horas, Fazia frio, Chovia.

Age uses ter, which says literally I had ten years, the same structure as the present tenho trinta anos. Time uses ser in the plural or the singular according to the noun, just as in the present: São duas horas becomes Eram duas horas, and É uma hora becomes Era uma hora, with Era meio-dia for noon. The weather verbs are fazer (literally it made: Fazia frio, It made cold), chover (Chovia, regular, and normally used only in the third person singular) and estar (Estava frio). The existential tem, there is, becomes tinha: Tem um parque becomes Tinha um parque, and the formal há becomes havia. In Naquela época, não tinha internet, tinha has no subject and means there was.

Contrast with English: where English chooses between used to, would and the simple past, Portuguese keeps the imperfect and lets the context carry the habit. The English would is also a conditional (I would go if I could), which Portuguese expresses with a different form that you will meet later. A one-time completed event in the same scene needs the preterite, which the next unit contrasts with the imperfect in detail; here we only need to know that anything seen as a repeated, ongoing or descriptive state uses the imperfect.

a repeated action with no single end
a situation going on in the past
a state at a past moment
the state of the clock, plural to agree with horas

something existed, as in there was

grammar.title: Costumar, sempre and the words that point to a habit
grammar.explanation:
The imperfect already says habit by itself, so the extra words are optional help, not requirements. Adverbs are words that add information about an action, such as when, how often or how it happens. The ones that tell when or how often cluster around the imperfect: sempre (always), todo dia (every day), toda semana, de vez em quando, às vezes (sometimes) and nunca (never). Expressions that set the time are quando eu era criança, antigamente, naquela época, na minha infância and no meu tempo. Eu nunca comia peixe is complete on its own, and these words only make it explicit.

To make the habit unmistakable, use costumar in the imperfect followed directly by an infinitive: Eu costumava acordar às seis. This is the closest equivalent of used to, and it is built on costume, a custom. The present tense is costumo, which means usually, not used to: Eu costumo acordar cedo is a present habit, and Eu costumava acordar cedo is a past one. In practice the simple imperfect is often more natural (Eu acordava às seis), and costumava is most useful when the contrast with the present is the point.

Two small details of structure are worth knowing. Todo without an article means every (todo dia, every day), while todo after the article means the whole of it (o dia todo, the whole day, all day long), so Chovia o tempo todo is it rained all the time and Meu pai trabalhava todo dia is my father worked every day. And Portuguese says quando eu era criança, with no article, where English says when I was a child. The structure is when I was child, because criança here names a stage of life, as in a profession.

grammar.title: The imperfect progressive: estava plus the gerund
grammar.explanation:
To show what was in progress at one particular moment, Portuguese combines two verbs. The first is estar in the imperfect (estava), an auxiliary verb: a helper that carries the tense and the person. The second is the gerund, a verb form that ends in -ndo and carries the meaning, like the -ing form in English. The gerund never changes for gender or number, and only estar changes: eu estava falando, ela estava falando, nós estávamos falando, eles estavam falando. The accent on estávamos follows the stress rule of the spelling note. In Brazil this is the only pattern, estava falando, while European Portuguese uses estava a falar.

The gerund is made by removing the infinitive ending and adding -ando to -ar verbs, -endo to -er verbs and -indo to -ir verbs. The vowel is the vowel of the family, and the n makes the vowel before it nasal, so falando is pronounced fa-LÃ-du with no separate n sound. The stress sits on the syllable before -do, which is second to last, so no accent is needed. Pôr has the irregular gerund pondo. The gerund is also narrower than the English -ing: where English says swimming is fun, Portuguese uses the infinitive (nadar é bom).

How does the progressive differ from the plain imperfect? Às oito eu jantava and Às oito eu estava jantando are both correct, but the progressive pictures the action unfolding at that instant and is the usual choice when you describe a scene, a photograph or a memory: A gente estava soprando as velas. Verbs of state do not normally go into the progressive, because a state is not an action that unfolds: say Eu tinha dez anos, not estava tendo dez anos. Finally, English says had been cooking since early morning, using a special past perfect progressive, while Portuguese says simply estava cozinhando desde cedo. The next unit combines this background action with a sudden event in the preterite.

culture.title: Brincadeiras de rua and saudade
culture.text:
For many Brazilians who grew up before smartphones, childhood meant playing in the street until the streetlights came on. Classic games are pega-pega (tag, literally catch-catch), esconde-esconde (hide and seek, literally hide-hide), amarelinha (hopscotch, literally little yellow one), bolinha de gude (marbles, literally little ball of gude, a word found almost only in this name), soltar pipa (flying kites, literally to release kite) and, of course, futebol with a ball made of anything at all. Parents would call the children home for dinner, often shouting from the window, and neighbors treated the whole street as a shared playground.

School followed its own rhythm. Public schools usually have two shifts, morning and afternoon, so a child would go to school either from seven to noon or from one to six. The recreio was the best part of the day, when kids ate their merenda, which could be a sandwich from home or a plate served at the school. Uniforms are common in both public and private schools. Many Brazilians remember television shows such as Sítio do Picapau Amarelo (literally Farm of the Yellow Woodpecker) and Turma da Mônica (Monica's Gang), which are still popular today.

Talking about the past almost always leads to the word saudade. It means missing a person, a place or a time, often with a mix of sweetness and sadness. People say Tenho saudade da minha infância, Que saudade daquele tempo or simply Saudade! Many Brazilians consider it a very characteristic word of their culture, and it appears in countless songs and poems. Notice that the imperfect is the tense of saudade: it is the inside view of the past, a time that was going on and is remembered without its end, which is exactly the feeling the word describes.

paragraphs.pt: Eu nasci numa cidade pequena no interior de Goiás. Naquela época, tinha só uma praça, uma igreja e uma escola. Todo mundo se conhecia e as portas ficavam abertas.
paragraphs.en: I was born in a small town in the interior of Goiás. At that time, there was only a square, a church and a school. Everybody knew each other and the doors stayed open.
paragraphs.literal: I was-born in-a city small in-the interior of Goiás. In-that era, had only a square, a church and a school. All world themselves knew and the doors stayed open.

paragraphs.pt: Depois da escola, eu brincava na rua com os vizinhos. A gente jogava bola e soltava pipa. Minha mãe chamava a gente pra jantar quando escurecia.
paragraphs.en: After school, I played in the street with the neighbors. We played ball and flew kites. My mother called us to dinner when it got dark.
paragraphs.literal: After of-the school, I played in-the street with the neighbors. The-people played ball and released kite. My mother called the-people to dine when it-got-dark.

paragraphs.pt: Hoje a cidade é grande, tem muitas lojas e internet rápida. Mas eu ainda tenho muita saudade daquele tempo.
paragraphs.en: Today the town is big, with many shops and fast internet. But I still miss that time a lot.
paragraphs.literal: Today the city is big, has many shops and internet fast. But I still have much longing of-that time.

exercises.prompt: Match each imperfect form with its meaning
Why does falávamos carry a written accent while the present falamos does not?
choices: Because every plural verb form takes an accent
Because the á marks the imperfect tense
Because falávamos is stressed on the third to last syllable, but a word ending in os is expected to be stressed on the second to last
exercises.explanation: The imperfect adds a syllable, so the stress ends up third from the end. That breaks the default for the ending, so an accent is written. Falamos is stressed second to last, which is the default.

exercises.prompt: Which verb form presents living somewhere in the past as an ongoing state, with no start or end in view?
exercises.explanation: The imperfect (morava) is the inside view of the past. The preterite morei sees the living as one completed event.

exercises.prompt_pt: Quando eu era criança, a gente ___ na rua todo dia.
exercises.hint_en: When I was a child, we played in the street every day. (brincar)
exercises.explanation: A gente takes the same form as ele, and -ar verbs form the imperfect with -ava.

exercises.prompt: Why does ia have no accent while íamos does?
choices: Because the í marks the plural
Because ia is stressed second to last, which is the default for a word ending in a, while íamos is stressed third to last
exercises.explanation: Ia is I-a, and íamos is Í-a-mos. A stress on the third to last syllable always needs an accent.

exercises.hint_en: We used to walk to school. (ir)
exercises.explanation: Ir takes the -ia ending in the imperfect, and the nós form adds a syllable and an accent: íamos.

exercises.explanation: Portuguese expresses age with ter, literally I had ten years. The imperfect is used because age is a state seen from inside.

exercises.prompt: Why is the verb plural in Eram duas horas?
choices: It agrees with the plural noun horas, as São duas horas does in the present
It agrees with the person speaking
The imperfect of ser is always plural for time
exercises.explanation: Era uma hora has a singular noun, so it has a singular verb. Eram duas horas has a plural noun, so it has a plural verb.

exercises.hint_en: My mother used to put sugar in everything. (pôr)
exercises.explanation: Pôr is one of the four irregular verbs: stem pun- plus the ending -a, so punha.

exercises.explanation: Costumo is the present tense and means usually. Costumava and the plain imperfect refer to the past.

Because the u marks a nasal vowel

exercises.prompt: Why is saía (he or she used to leave) written with an accent on the í?
choices: Because saía is stressed on the third to last syllable
Because the í marks a nasal vowel
Because a stressed i after another vowel stands alone in its syllable and is not a diphthong
Because the accent marks the imperfect tense
exercises.explanation: Sa-Í-a has three syllables with the stress on the second, which is the default for a word ending in a. The accent is there because the stressed i follows the vowel a and must not be read as a glide; without it, saia would be the skirt.

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of the nós form of comer in the imperfect?
exercises.explanation: Co-MÍ-a-mos is stressed on the third to last syllable, which breaks the default for a word ending in os, so the accent goes on the stressed vowel, the i.

exercises.prompt: In which word is the qu pronounced with a w sound, as in English quick?
exercises.explanation: Qu before e or i is normally the k sound with a silent u. Qu before a or o keeps the u as a w sound, so only quando has it.

exercises.hint_en: My grandparents lived in the countryside. (morar)
exercises.explanation: The plural subject takes the ending -am, added to the imperfect form: morava becomes moravam. The stress stays on the same a, second to last, so no accent is needed.

exercises.prompt: Why is Eu estava tendo dez anos not Portuguese for I was ten years old?

Because estava can only be used with -ar verbs
Because the progressive needs the preterite
exercises.explanation: The progressive shows an action in progress. Age is a state, so the imperfect of ter is used: Eu tinha dez anos.
